title: Shohei Ohtani returns to Dodgers lineup after 4-game absence
content:
LOS ANGELES — Shohei Ohtani strolled into the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse at 2:30 p.m. on Monday, slipped into workout gear and resumed his season after a four-game absence from the reigning back-to-back World Series champions.

Ohtani, who has not played since appearing physically compromised on Wednesday against the St. Louis Cardinals, returned to the leadoff spot as the designated hitter on Monday. The four-time MVP reported enough improvement in his nagging left knee, right biceps and neck injuries to warrant returning to the lineup for the final 19 games of the regular season as a hitter.

“I do think these last four days, giving his body a reset, giving his mind a reset — anything can happen tonight as far as performance, but I’m hoping that he’s just in a better state (with his) body and mind tonight,” manager Dave Roberts said.

The four consecutive missed games were the longest time Ohtani had been out of the Dodgers’ lineup since signing with the club ahead of the 2024 season, and reflect the hurdles that have come with Ohtani pursuing his first full-time two-way season since 2023.

Those plans are all but kaput. The Dodgers have “put a pin” on Ohtani pitching, hoping that the reduced workload keeps him healthy and productive in the lineup. Roberts declined to say Ohtani would not pitch again in 2026, but the calendar all but rules it out. There is no timetable for Ohtani to pick up what might be a futile attempt at a throwing progression after he last pitched in a big league game on July 3.

“I’m choosing not to say it’s dead,” Roberts said of Ohtani’s pitching plans.

It remains unclear how Ohtani himself feels physically or how he took the news that his pitching was on pause. Monday marked three weeks since he last spoke to reporters, despite multiple requests through a Dodgers public relations official.

The Dodgers won all four games without Ohtani in the lineup as other figures in their star-studded lineup such as Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman and Teoscar Hernández have put together their share of offensive moments. The morass the lineup played through for much of July and August has subsided in September as the Dodgers have played lesser opponents.

Still, it is difficult to argue that Ohtani’s biggest impact for the Dodgers going forward is with his bat.

“I think he’s our best hitter,” Roberts said of Ohtani, whose 30 home runs and .906 OPS at the plate this season can be considered a disappointment only when compared to the consecutive historic 50-homer seasons that preceded it.

Ohtani’s four-day hiatus was largely about getting him back to the best version of himself at the plate. He had six hits in his last 46 at-bats before being shut down, including a hitless night where he struck out four times against the Cardinals and was shaking his arm out between each swing by the end of the night.

The Dodgers minimized his workload on Thursday, had him swinging in the cage by Saturday and, in the eighth inning Sunday, had him going over scouting reports with interpreter Will Ireton to prepare for a potential pinch-hit appearance. If anything reflected how good Ohtani felt after the respite, it was the 32-year-old star jokingly asking Roberts if the manager wanted him to pinch-run during Sunday’s 7-5 win over the Washington Nationals.
